title: Selective Laser Melting of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloy Powders: A Review

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Fundamentals of Selective Laser Melting
subsections.subsection_title: Magnesium Alloys and Powders as Emerging Feedstocks
subsections.content:
Magnesium and its alloys are increasingly viewed as distinctive feedstocks for powder-based manufacturing because they combine the lowest density among structural metallic materials with attractive specific strength and, in selected chemistries, functional biodegradability for biomedical use. Their lightweighting potential has driven renewed interest in transportation and aerospace applications, while the possibility of fabricating resorbable devices has expanded attention in the medical field ref [1], ref [3], ref [8]. For additive routes such as selective laser melting (SLM), these attributes make Mg powders strategically important despite their narrower processing window compared with more established Al, Ti, or stainless-steel powders.

From a feedstock perspective, recent work has emphasized gas-atomized powders such as AZ91E, WE43, and Elektron21, which offer controlled particle morphology and rapid-solidification-derived microstructural refinement that can be advantageous for subsequent consolidation ref [1]. More broadly, powder metallurgy has already demonstrated that metastable or highly refined Mg alloy powders can unlock property combinations not readily attainable by conventional ingot processing. A notable example is rapidly solidified Mg97Zn1Y2 powder metallurgy material, which achieved tensile yield strengths above 600 MPa while retaining useful ductility, illustrating the broader promise of powder-based alloy design in Mg systems ref [2].

At the same time, magnesium powders present unusually stringent constraints for SLM feedstock qualification. High chemical reactivity, flammability, and sensitivity to oxidation demand careful control of powder production, storage, handling, and oxygen pickup, while alloy selection must also account for the well-known corrosion susceptibility of Mg in aqueous and physiological environments ref [7], ref [8]. These challenges are not merely limitations; they define the research space in which Mg powders are emerging. In particular, rare-earth-containing and Zn/Ca-containing compositions are being explored to balance printability, mechanical integrity, and degradation behavior for implant applications, where the biological appeal of Mg as a resorbable orthopedic material further strengthens its relevance as an emerging SLM feedstock ref [1], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Fundamentals of Selective Laser Melting
subsections.subsection_title: SLM of Biomedical and Implant Metals
subsections.content:
Selective laser melting (SLM) has become a major route for manufacturing metallic implants because it combines near-net-shape fabrication with geometric freedom for patient-specific devices and controlled porous architectures. Among established implant metals, Ti alloys, 316L stainless steel, and Co–Cr alloys are the principal powder-bed feedstocks, with Ti-6Al-4V being the most extensively studied owing to its favorable strength-to-weight ratio, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility ref [7]. For orthopaedic applications, powder-bed AM is particularly attractive because lattice and graded-porosity designs can be integrated directly into implants to promote osseointegration and reduce stress shielding relative to fully dense conventionally manufactured parts ref [7].

Titanium has served as the benchmark biomedical metal for SLM. Beyond commercially pure Ti and Ti-6Al-4V, the literature has expanded toward Ti-6Al-7Nb, metastable beta-Ti alloys such as Ti-24Nb-4Zr-8Sn, and Ti-based matrix composites, motivated by the need for lower elastic modulus, improved wear resistance, and elimination of potentially unfavorable alloying elements ref [6]. A recurring observation is that the rapid solidification inherent to SLM produces distinctive nonequilibrium microstructures and high strength, while post-processing is often required to tailor residual stress, anisotropy, and fatigue behavior for long-term implant service ref [6].

These developments in biomedical Ti, stainless steel, and Co–Cr systems provide the conceptual foundation for considering Mg and Mg-alloy powders in SLM-based implant manufacturing. The key lesson is that success is governed not only by biocompatibility, but also by the coupling among powder characteristics, process window, porosity design, and microstructure-sensitive properties such as corrosion, stiffness, and fatigue ref [6], ref [7]. In this context, the experience accumulated for established implant metals offers an important framework for evaluating whether SLM can enable biodegradable Mg implants with patient-specific geometry and mechanically compatible architectures.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Fundamentals of Selective Laser Melting
subsections.subsection_title: Overview of Selective Laser Melting and Metal Additive Manufacturing
subsections.content:
Metal additive manufacturing (AM) comprises a family of layer-wise fabrication routes in which digital geometry is translated into three-dimensional components through the successive consolidation of metallic feedstock. Within this broader landscape, powder-bed and directed-energy processes are the dominant laser-based approaches, while selective laser melting (SLM), often grouped with laser powder bed fusion, is distinguished by the near-complete melting of thin powder layers using a scanning laser beam under inert atmosphere ref [9], ref [10]. More generally, laser processing inherits the fundamental advantages of high energy density, precise spatial controllability, and localized thermal input that have long underpinned welding, cladding, and related materials-processing technologies ref [11].

Compared with subtractive manufacturing, SLM offers exceptional geometric freedom, high material utilization, and the ability to produce internal channels, lattice structures, and patient-specific or lightweight parts directly from CAD data ref [8], ref [9]. These advantages have driven rapid adoption across aerospace, tooling, automotive, and biomedical sectors, especially where low-volume, high-complexity components are needed ref [8], ref [10]. At the same time, SLM differs from conventional powder metallurgy because shaping and densification occur simultaneously, creating a highly nonequilibrium thermal history with repeated melting, solidification, and reheating on a voxel-by-voxel and layer-by-layer basis ref [9], ref [10].

From a process-science perspective, SLM performance is governed by the coupled effects of laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, powder characteristics, and scan strategy, all of which determine melt-pool stability, defect formation, residual stress, and final microstructure ref [8], ref [9]. Accordingly, the technology is best viewed not simply as a shaping method, but as a rapid solidification route in which processing, metallurgy, and part performance are tightly linked ref [8], ref [10]. This perspective is particularly important for magnesium and its alloys, whose low boiling point, high reactivity, and flammability narrow the processing window relative to more established implant and structural metals.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Fundamentals of Selective Laser Melting
subsections.subsection_title: Fundamental Process Physics and Melt Track Formation
subsections.content:
At the melt-track scale, selective laser melting is governed by coupled phenomena including laser absorption by a loose powder bed, rapid heat conduction into previously solidified material, melting and re-melting of particles, capillarity-driven wetting, recoil-pressure-induced vaporization, and thermocapillary convection within the molten pool ref [13], ref [14]. Relative to bulk metals, powder beds typically exhibit higher effective absorptance because of multiple scattering and repeated internal reflections among particles, so local packing state, particle morphology, and oxidation condition directly influence energy coupling and track initiation ref [4]. These mechanisms are especially consequential for magnesium alloys, whose high reflectivity, low boiling point, and strong vaporization tendency narrow the stable processing window.

Single-track studies show that continuous bead formation is the primary prerequisite for dense multilayer builds ref [13]. When the supplied energy is too low, incomplete melting and poor wetting produce discontinuous, balling-dominated tracks; when it is excessive, evaporation, spatter, denudation, and unstable keyhole-like behavior promote geometric irregularity and defect formation ref [12], ref [13]. Track stability is therefore controlled not by laser power alone, but by the combined effects of power, scan speed, layer thickness, hatch spacing, and substrate thermal state, which determine melt-pool aspect ratio and overlap between adjacent vectors ref [13], ref [14].

From a metallurgical perspective, the transition from bonding to full melting is central to SLM process physics. Kruth et al. distinguished partial melting, liquid-phase sintering, and complete melting as different binding regimes, with fully dense SLM requiring sufficient liquid formation to ensure wetting and consolidation between particles and across layers ref [12]. Because solidification rates are extremely high, melt tracks develop steep thermal gradients and fine cellular or dendritic substructures, while repeated thermal cycling alters epitaxial growth and local segregation ref [14]. Consequently, optimization of magnesium SLM must begin with stable single-track formation, since melt-track continuity ultimately governs densification, pore inheritance, and the microstructural path followed during layer-by-layer build-up.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Fundamentals of Selective Laser Melting
subsections.subsection_title: Process Control, Densification, and Microstructure Development
subsections.content:
Process control in SLM is fundamentally aimed at stabilizing melt-pool behavior and balancing energy input against the high thermal gradients intrinsic to powder-bed fusion. Densification is commonly rationalized through the combined effects of laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, and scan strategy, which together determine whether lack-of-fusion pores or keyhole/gas porosity dominate. In AlSi10Mg, careful parameter optimization and scan-strategy selection were shown to reduce porosity and achieve relative densities approaching 99.8%, illustrating the narrow but usable processing window relevant to light metals more broadly, including Mg alloys with even higher volatility and oxidation sensitivity [2].

Powder characteristics add a second layer of control. Particle morphology, size distribution, packing density, and flowability influence layer uniformity, laser absorptivity, and melt-track continuity. Evidence from SLM Ti-TiB composites indicates that powder particle shape measurably affects consolidation behavior and final properties, underscoring that feedstock engineering is not secondary to parameter optimization [3]. For magnesium powders, this implication is especially important because irregular spreading, oxide films, and vaporization-induced spatter can readily interrupt melt-track stability, promote balling, and lower densification.

Microstructure development is governed by repeated rapid melting and solidification, giving rise to fine cellular or dendritic structures, strong epitaxial grain growth, and pronounced texture in many alloys. The resulting microstructure depends not only on local cooling rate but also on remelting between adjacent tracks and successive layers, so scan rotation and thermal history become practical microstructural control tools. For Mg and Mg-alloy SLM, these relationships are expected to be amplified by the metal's low boiling point and high chemical reactivity, making dense part production contingent on strict atmosphere control, moderated volumetric energy density, and powder/feedstock quality management in addition to nominal laser settings [2].

subsections.section_title: Processing Windows and Quantitative Processing Data for Magnesium Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Magnesium AM Processing Windows in Powder Bed Fusion
subsections.content:
In powder bed fusion of magnesium, the processing window is unusually narrow because the material combines low boiling temperature, high vapor pressure, strong oxidation tendency, and low absorptivity at common laser wavelengths. Early work therefore focused on controlled-atmosphere miniaturized SLM systems and single-track experiments to determine whether stable melting could be achieved at all, showing that magnesium can be processed but only within a limited combination of laser power, scan speed, and irradiation mode ref [17], ref [18]. These studies established that process-window definition for Mg must be based not only on consolidation, but also on suppression of evaporation, balling, and oxygen pickup ref [17], ref [18].

A useful way to interpret the magnesium window is through melt-track stability. Ng et al. showed that both continuous-wave and pulsed Nd:YAG irradiation can generate Mg tracks, but track width, penetration depth, and surface condition vary sharply with energy input; excessive intensity promotes spatter, oxidation, and irregular bead morphologies, whereas insufficient input leads to discontinuous tracks and weak bonding ref [18]. Moving from single tracks to bulk parts, Hu et al. demonstrated that net-shape pure Mg can be produced by SLM only in a constrained region where near-full melting is achieved without severe vaporization-induced defects; outside this region, lack-of-fusion porosity at low input and instability/keyholing-like surface disruption at high input dominate ref [3].

Accordingly, magnesium PBF windows are typically centered on moderate linear or volumetric energy input, high-purity inert shielding, and careful balancing of layer thickness and hatch overlap rather than simply increasing power. The literature therefore suggests a hierarchical window-development strategy for Mg systems: first identify continuous single tracks, then overlap-stable scan lines, and finally dense multilayer builds under tightly controlled atmosphere ref [17], ref [18], ref [3]. This contrasts with more process-tolerant alloys and explains why magnesium PBF studies remain strongly parameter-sensitive and machine-specific.

subsections.section_title: Processing Windows and Quantitative Processing Data for Magnesium Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Quantitative Laser Processing Metrics and General Process Relationships
subsections.content:
Quantitative comparison of powder-bed fusion conditions for magnesium systems is commonly framed through the volumetric energy density, VED = P/(vht), where P is laser power, v scan speed, h hatch spacing, and t layer thickness. Although convenient for comparing nominal settings, this scalar metric is only a first-order descriptor because it neglects absorptivity, beam diameter, powder packing, melt-pool geometry, and vaporization losses; broad SLM reviews have emphasized that identical VED values can produce very different consolidation outcomes when parameter combinations differ substantially [2, ref 3, ref 4]. For Mg and Mg alloys, this limitation is especially important because low boiling temperature, high oxidation sensitivity, and strong process-induced evaporation make the coupling between delivered energy and actual melt enthalpy highly nonlinear [ref 1, ref 5].

General process relationships nevertheless follow the same trend structure observed across metal PBF: too little line energy or areal/volumetric energy input promotes lack-of-fusion porosity and discontinuous scan tracks, whereas excessive input enlarges the melt pool, intensifies recoil pressure and spatter, and can increase keyhole-like instability, denudation, composition change, and roughness [2, ref 3, ref 4, ref 6]. Stable processing therefore requires a constrained window balancing complete remelting of adjacent tracks and layers against overheating. Single-track and melt-pool based studies have shown that track continuity, width/depth ratio, overlap, and remelting depth are practical quantitative indicators of this balance and are often more transferable than VED alone when constructing magnesium processing maps [ref 4, ref 6, ref 7].

A useful magnesium-specific interpretation is to separate metrics by scale: power–speed combinations govern linear energy input and track stability; hatch spacing controls lateral overlap and pore closure; layer thickness sets the remelting burden; and scan strategy influences thermal accumulation and defect inheritance between layers [2, ref 3, ref 5, ref 8]. Accordingly, dense Mg builds are expected only within a narrow thermo-fluid regime in which the melt pool remains continuous but not excessively deep, oxidation is minimized by stringent atmosphere control, and evaporation-driven instability is suppressed. This perspective also aligns Mg PBF with broader laser processing science, where process maps based on normalized energy input, melt-pool dimensions, and defect mode transitions are increasingly preferred over sole reliance on VED [ref 3, ref 8, ref 9].

subsections.section_title: Processing Windows and Quantitative Processing Data for Magnesium Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Related Laser-Based Processing Routes and Comparative Context
subsections.content:
Selective laser melting (SLM) of Mg powders is best interpreted within the broader family of laser-based thermal processes. In contrast to powder-bed fusion, laser metal deposition (LMD) delivers powder directly into the melt pool and is typically used for near-net-shape build-up, cladding, or repair rather than for the finest feature resolution. From a powder-metallurgy perspective, LMD highlights the same core process variables—laser power, interaction time, powder characteristics, shielding, and melt-pool stability—but under substantially different thermal gradients, catchment efficiency, and bead-scale solidification conditions ref [19]. More general laser additive-manufacturing reviews likewise place powder-bed fusion and directed deposition on a continuum of energy-density-driven melting and rapid solidification, with process selection governed by the trade-off between geometric precision and deposition rate.

For magnesium specifically, laser welding provides an important comparative benchmark because it isolates laser–material interaction and melt-pool behavior without the added complexity of powder spreading. Sanders et al. showed for AZ31B that Nd:YAG welding gave better weldability than CO2 laser welding, attributing this to higher absorptivity, lower threshold irradiance for stable welding, and reduced weld-pool instability ref [3]. These observations are directly relevant to Mg powder-bed processing: the same low absorptivity, low viscosity, and low surface tension that complicate welding also narrow the stable processing window in SLM, while fume and particulate formation during welding foreshadow the evaporation and spatter issues commonly reported in Mg AM ref [3].

Thus, related laser routes provide useful comparative context for interpreting Mg SLM process windows. Welding studies clarify beam-wavelength sensitivity, keyhole/conduction mode transitions, and the consequences of Mg vaporization, whereas LMD studies emphasize powder delivery, metallurgical dilution, and repair-oriented process control ref [1,3]. For survey purposes, these adjacent processes should not be conflated with SLM, but they do supply transferable mechanistic insight into absorptivity-limited coupling, melt-pool stability, oxidation control, and defect formation in magnesium systems.

subsections.section_title: Performance Characteristics and Biomedical Structural Potential
subsections.content:
For biomedical SLM magnesium, mechanical suitability is judged less by maximizing absolute strength than by approaching the stiffness, deformation, and energy-absorption characteristics of bone while retaining sufficient load-bearing capacity. This perspective is important because dense metallic implants can induce stress shielding, whereas porous or architected metals reduce effective modulus and permit more favorable load transfer. Reviews of porous metals consistently show that stiffness and strength can be tuned through relative density, pore morphology, and connectivity, making structural analogy to cancellous bone a central design principle for implant lattices and scaffolds ref [24], ref [25]. Similar reasoning underlies the clinical interest in porous tantalum, whose open-cell architecture provides moderate compressive strength together with a compliant scaffold response suitable for early osseous support ref [23].

Within the magnesium family, composition and microstructural refinement provide an additional route to mechanical matching. For example, silica-nanoparticle reinforcement in magnesium was shown to reduce grain size and improve compressive yield strength, fracture strain, hardness, and damping, while producing only a limited change in elastic modulus; notably, the authors explicitly compared the resulting biomechanical window with natural bone ref [21]. This balance is particularly relevant to SLM Mg and Mg alloys, where rapid solidification commonly refines grains and can elevate strength, but where excessive densification without architectural control may leave the modulus still above that of trabecular bone. Accordingly, the most promising strategy is not simply stronger Mg, but microstructure-engineered and topology-engineered Mg with a compressive response closer to bone-like deformation behavior ref [21], ref [24].

The structural analogy should also be considered at the microdamage level. Bone remodeling is strongly linked to local strain amplification around microstructural features, and finite-element analysis has shown that microdamage near osteocyte lacunae can alter local strain fields sufficiently to trigger remodeling-related responses ref [22]. This insight suggests that SLM magnesium implants should be evaluated not only by bulk modulus and strength, but also by how their pore architecture, anisotropy, and defect population shape local stress concentrations under cyclic loading. Evidence from porous tantalum and directionally porous metals shows that cell geometry and pore orientation govern fatigue resistance, crack initiation sites, and anisotropic deformation modes ref [23], ref [25]. For SLM Mg scaffolds, these analogies support the design of mechanically graded architectures that better emulate bone’s hierarchical load transfer rather than relying on monolithic solid sections alone ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Performance Characteristics and Biomedical Structural Potential
subsections.content:
Corrosion in physiological media is the central constraint on the biomedical use of SLM-fabricated Mg and Mg alloys, because degradation must remain sufficiently slow and spatially uniform to preserve early-stage mechanical support. In chloride-containing aqueous environments, Mg dissolution is accompanied by hydrogen evolution and the formation of only partially protective surface films, so localized attack can readily develop once the film is disrupted or galvanically undermined by microstructural heterogeneities ref [26], ref [27], ref [28]. For additively manufactured materials, this issue is amplified by process-induced features such as unmelted particles, oxide-rich boundaries, porosity, and evaporation-driven solute redistribution, all of which can create local electrochemical cells and accelerate nonuniform degradation.

Biomedical electrolytes are more aggressive than simple saline because they contain buffering species, calcium- and phosphate-bearing ions, and proteins that continuously modify surface films and corrosion products. Electrochemical studies in simulated body fluid have shown that corrosion resistance of Mg rare-earth alloys is markedly lower in m-SBF than in isotonic NaCl, that albumin can transiently block the surface during the first hours, and that the resulting amorphous apatite-containing layers possess limited protective ability ref [29]. More broadly, current understanding indicates that body-fluid chemistry strongly controls film stability, local alkalization, and corrosion morphology; accordingly, Nor's solution and related model media have been proposed as useful platforms for systematically isolating the role of individual constituents during implant degradation ref [26].

For SLM Mg biomaterials, the practical target is therefore not absolute corrosion resistance but a predictable biodegradation profile matched to tissue healing. This requires minimizing impurity-driven cathodic activity, controlling second-phase continuity, and tailoring surface condition after fabrication, since purification and microstructural control can substantially reduce corrosion susceptibility in Mg systems ref [26], ref [27], ref [28]. At the same time, in vitro assessment should be interpreted cautiously: electrochemical responses, hydrogen evolution, and corrosion-layer formation are time dependent and medium sensitive, so meaningful qualification of SLM implants demands test protocols that better reproduce dynamic biomedical environments ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Performance Characteristics and Biomedical Structural Potential
subsections.subsection_title: Surface and Laser-Based Modification for Performance Enhancement
subsections.content:
Surface engineering is especially important for SLM-fabricated Mg because the process can generate rough, chemically heterogeneous surfaces that accelerate localized attack, even when the bulk microstructure is refined. Laser-based post-treatment is attractive in this context because it can remelt only the near-surface region, reducing micro-galvanic heterogeneity while preserving the geometric freedom of additively manufactured implants. Early studies on AZ61 and AZ91 showed that laser-assisted surface modification substantially altered the surface and subsurface microstructure relative to the cast state and improved resistance to localized corrosion in chloride solution, primarily through redistribution or suppression of deleterious secondary precipitates and formation of a more homogeneous remelted layer ref [30].

Comparable effects were later reported for rare-earth-containing WE43, where laser surface melting produced a refined resolidified layer with modified phase distribution and measurably improved corrosion behavior relative to the untreated alloy ref [31]. In biomaterials-oriented Mg-Mn systems, the combination of Mn alloying and rapid laser melting further increased corrosion potential, refined grains, and enhanced hardness/compressive response, indicating that laser processing can simultaneously tune degradation and mechanical integrity when composition and remelting conditions are co-optimized ref [32]. These observations are highly relevant to SLM Mg alloys, whose as-built microstructures already reflect rapid solidification; localized laser remelting may therefore serve as a secondary microstructural homogenization step rather than merely a polishing operation.

For biomedical use, the key implication is that laser-based surface modification offers a route to spatially controlled performance: high-risk regions such as struts, junctions, or threaded features could be selectively remelted to delay premature pitting, while other regions retain faster biodegradation. Such strategies may also complement subsequent coatings or chemical conversion layers by first reducing roughness, porosity opening, and galvanically active phase contrast at the surface ref [30], ref [31]. Overall, laser remelting should be viewed as an enabling pre-treatment for SLM Mg implants, capable of coupling corrosion moderation with local mechanical strengthening, although systematic studies on true SLM-built Mg scaffolds remain limited ref [31], ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Performance Characteristics and Biomedical Structural Potential
subsections.subsection_title: Additive Manufacturing, Residual Stress, and Implant Design Potential
subsections.content:
For magnesium and magnesium alloys, selective laser melting (SLM) is attractive not only because it can consolidate highly reactive powders into near-net-shape components, but also because it enables geometries that are difficult to realize by conventional processing, including controlled lattice architectures and patient-specific implant forms. More broadly, powder-bed fusion has been recognized as a key route for metallic implant fabrication because it permits direct translation of medical imaging into customized structures, graded porosity, and topology-optimized load paths that can reduce stress shielding while promoting tissue integration ref [7]. These design freedoms are especially relevant to biodegradable Mg systems, where structural layout can be used alongside alloy selection to tune both mechanical support and degradation kinetics.

A central challenge is residual stress generation during SLM. Steep thermal gradients, cyclic reheating, and constrained shrinkage induce nonuniform internal stresses that depend on scan strategy, geometry, and section thickness; early experimental work using the hole-drilling method showed that residual stress distributions in SLM parts are spatially heterogeneous and strongly process dependent ref [33]. In Mg alloys, such stresses are of particular concern because they can aggravate distortion, microcrack susceptibility, and local corrosion heterogeneity after implantation. Consequently, residual-stress-aware process design—through optimized hatch rotation, energy density control, platform preheating, and post-processing—should be considered integral to biomedical qualification rather than a secondary manufacturing issue.

From an implant-design perspective, additive manufacturing therefore offers two coupled opportunities for Mg-based biomaterials: architectural control of stiffness and permeability, and local control of thermal history and stress state. Reviews of metallic implant AM emphasize that interconnected porosity, surface topography, and patient-specific external morphology can be co-designed to improve osteo-inductive performance and biomechanical compatibility ref [7]. For biodegradable Mg implants, this implies that lattice size, strut thickness, and density gradients may be deliberately selected to emulate bone-like load transfer while compensating for time-dependent material loss. The remaining challenge is to integrate these design advantages with robust control of residual stress and dimensional fidelity, so that mechanically efficient and biologically responsive Mg implant concepts can be translated into clinically reliable devices ref [33], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Performance Characteristics and Biomedical Structural Potential
subsections.content:
The relevance of SLM-fabricated Mg scaffolds to bone substitution is best understood by comparison with the hierarchical porosity and remodeling dynamics of native bone. Cortical bone contains distinct pore populations, notably Haversian canals and osteocytic lacunae, and its porosity increases with age primarily through enlargement and prevalence of vascular canals rather than lacunar changes ref [34]. This distinction is important for Mg implant design: engineered porosity should not merely reduce stiffness, but should also approximate transport pathways and local stress environments that support cell viability and tissue integration. At the trabecular scale, bone further operates as a mechanically efficient open-cell architecture, suggesting that additively manufactured Mg lattices can be tuned to mimic both stiffness and permeability if pore size, interconnectivity, and strut dimensions are appropriately controlled.

Bone is also a continuously adapting tissue, in which resorption and formation coexist spatially and temporally. Histologic observations in periodontal lesions showed that even in inflammatory bone defects, peripheral walls may exhibit active apposition while adjacent regions undergo resorption, underscoring the localized and nonuniform nature of remodeling ref [35]. For biodegradable Mg structures, this is highly consequential: implant degradation should ideally proceed in balance with region-specific new bone formation rather than outpace it. Thus, SLM offers a useful platform because graded architectures, surface state control, and site-specific geometry can be used to tailor mechanical stimulus and corrosion kinetics toward remodeling-compatible healing.

From a design standpoint, the analogy between bone microstructure and AM Mg implants should therefore be treated as functional rather than purely geometric. Matching elastic response alone is insufficient; favorable osteointegration also depends on fluid access, interfacial surface area, and degradation-assisted load transfer as healing progresses. Consequently, bone-inspired SLM Mg implants are most promising when they reproduce key microstructural cues of cortical/trabecular bone while accommodating the dynamic coupling among porosity evolution, corrosion, and adaptive remodeling ref [34], ref [35].
